title: SmartDesk has no frontend
content: Worth writing down because I keep getting asked. SmartDesk is not a web app. It is an ADK agent served by adk web locally and deployed to Cloud Run as an HTTP service. The interface is the ADK dev UI or a plain HTTP request. There is no custom frontend and building one is not currently planned.

title: Agent architecture decision
content: Settled on a root orchestrator with three sub-agents rather than one agent with many tools. Root handles auth and routing via transfer_to_agent. inbox_agent covers Gmail, planner_agent covers Calendar, data_agent covers the AlloyDB knowledge base. Reason: one agent with fifteen tools kept picking the wrong tool. Splitting by domain made routing reliable.

title: Why ADK and not a custom loop
content: Considered writing my own orchestration loop. ADK gives sub-agent transfer, session state, and tool calling for free, which is most of what I would have had to build. The cost is ADK's opinionated state model and some surprising behaviour around when the loop terminates. Net: worth it for a solo project on a deadline.

title: Duplicate response bug
content: SmartDesk was answering the same question twice. Cause: after a sub-agent finishes, control returns to the root agent, which reprocesses the original prompt. Returning content=None does not stop the ADK loop, it retries. Fix is a before_model_callback that checks a _transferred flag and returns an empty text response, which ends the turn. Took most of a day to find.

title: MCP servers run as stdio subprocesses
content: Gmail and Calendar are self-hosted MCP servers launched by ADK as child processes via StdioConnectionParams. Originally tried the hosted HTTP MCP endpoints but they needed auth I did not have. Running them locally as scripts means I control the OAuth flow and can debug by reading stdout.

title: OAuth token storage is a problem
content: Tokens are currently written to a JSON file on the Cloud Run instance. That is ephemeral, unencrypted beyond platform default, and worst of all process-wide, so two users on the same instance could share credentials. For a single-user personal project this is tolerable. If anyone else ever uses it, this must move to Secret Manager keyed per user first.

title: Cloud Run cold start problem
content: First request after idle took 8-12 seconds. Cause: the container image was 1.8GB so scaling from zero meant pulling the whole thing. Switched to a slim Python base image, down to 340MB. Cold start now around 1.4s. Did not set minimum instances because that costs money continuously and this is a personal project.

title: AlloyDB is too expensive to leave running
content: AlloyDB bills continuously whether or not I use it. Left it running for a week during development and it was the single largest line on the bill. Now I only start it when actively testing against it, and develop against Postgres with pgvector locally. The schema and the distance operator are identical so the code does not care.

title: Local Postgres mirrors AlloyDB
content: Development runs on Postgres 16 with the pgvector extension in Docker, same schema as AlloyDB. The one incompatibility is AlloyDB's in-database embedding() function, which stock Postgres does not have. Solved by computing embeddings client-side and binding the vector as a parameter, which works on both.

title: Vector search returns nothing bug
content: Notes search silently returned zero results for every query. Cause: a batch of rows had null content_embedding after a failed insert, and the ORDER BY put nulls last but LIMIT 5 was being consumed by them. Fixed by adding a NOT NULL filter to the retrieval query and backfilling. Found it by accident, not by any monitoring.

title: Embedding dimension mismatch
content: Ingestion failed with a dimension error. Cause: I had SMARTDESK_EMBEDDER set to the local 384-dimension model from an earlier session, then ran ingestion against the database where the column is VECTOR(768). Nothing was corrupted because the insert failed atomically. Added an assertion that the embedder dimension matches the column before any write.

title: Retrieval quality is unmeasured
content: I have no idea whether search_notes is any good. There is no labelled set and no metric, so every change to chunking or ranking would be a guess. Decided to build an evaluation harness before touching retrieval at all. Recall at k as the main metric since the agent reads several results, MRR as secondary since the first result matters most to the model.

title: Notes on chunking
content: Whole-document embedding breaks down when a document covers several topics, because one vector has to represent all of them and ends up near none. Fixed-size chunking splits mid-sentence and makes citations read badly. Sentence-aligned chunks with token overlap is the usual compromise. Overlap costs storage roughly in proportion to the overlap fraction.

title: Notes on reranking options
content: Cross-encoders score the query and document together and are much more accurate than comparing two independent vectors, but cost one model call per candidate. BM25 is nearly free and catches rare exact terms that embeddings smooth over. Reciprocal rank fusion combines rankings without needing the score scales to match. Using an LLM directly is the most accurate and most expensive.

title: Embedding model choice
content: Using text-embedding-005 at 768 dimensions. Compared against 004 and the multilingual variant. 005 is better on English technical text, which is all my notes are. Multilingual scored worse on this domain. Would need to revisit only if I start keeping notes in another language.

title: No vector index yet
content: Considered IVFFlat and HNSW for the notes embedding column. At my corpus size a sequential scan is fast enough and exact, whereas approximate indexes trade recall for speed I do not need. Decision: no index until the corpus is past roughly 10,000 rows, then benchmark HNSW against exact search on the eval set.

title: Gemini model choice

Cost per conversation is well under a cent. Would only move to pro if the natural language work needed deeper reasoning.

title: Cost of running SmartDesk
content: Per conversation SmartDesk makes roughly three model calls at a couple of thousand input tokens each. At Flash pricing that is a fraction of a cent. Embeddings are written once per note so they are negligible. The real cost risk is not the model, it is an agent loop that does not terminate, which the callback guard now prevents.

title: Deployment to Cloud Run
content: Deployed as a container to Cloud Run in us-central1, same region as the Vertex endpoints to avoid cross-region latency. The service account needs Vertex AI user and AlloyDB client roles. Deploy is a single gcloud run deploy from source. Scaling to zero is what keeps this affordable when nobody is using it.

title: Environment variables that matter
content: GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI must be TRUE or the SDK tries the Gemini API instead of Vertex and fails on credentials. GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT and GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION need to match where the model is available. DATABASE_URL points at AlloyDB in production and local Postgres in development, which is the only line that changes between the two.

title: Testing without cloud credentials
content: Most development happens with no GCP credentials at all, using a local embedding model and local Postgres. This is deliberate: it means I can work on retrieval on a laptop without spending anything or waiting on a cloud database to start. The embedder is pluggable specifically to make this possible.

title: What I actually learned building this
content: The agent framework was the easy part. The hard parts were all at the edges: OAuth token scoping, the ADK loop not terminating on a null response, and the fact that a retrieval system will happily return confident nonsense with no signal that anything is wrong. Measurement turned out to matter more than any single technique.

title: Reading on retrieval evaluation
content: Recall at k answers whether the right document is in the set the model reads. MRR answers whether it is near the top, which matters because models weight the first thing they read heavily. Both are needed. A system can have excellent recall and still answer badly if the right document is consistently ranked fifth.

title: Managing four inboxes
content: Four accounts is too many but splitting them is still better than one inbox with everything. The rule that makes it work: each account has exactly one job, and I never sign up for something on the wrong account just because I happen to be logged in. When I break that rule I lose an hour later trying to find the login.

title: Deadline tracking across platforms
content: Deadlines are scattered across Hack2Skills, DoraHacks, the patent timeline, and job application follow-ups, each on a different account. Nothing aggregates them. This is genuinely the problem SmartDesk is supposed to solve for me, which is the honest reason I am building it rather than a hypothetical user need.

title: Working in Claude Code web sessions
content: Doing most of the development in Claude Code web sessions rather than locally, because the laptop is 16GB with no GPU and I would rather not run heavy things on it. Consequence: anything worth keeping has to be committed and pushed before the session ends, because the container is thrown away.

title: Why notes, contacts, and tasks
content: The knowledge base has three tables because those are the three things I actually look up. Notes for what happened and what was decided. Contacts for who someone is and where I met them. Tasks for what is outstanding. Only notes need vector search; contacts and tasks are fine with pattern matching and filters.

title: Contacts lookup is exact matching
content: get_contacts uses ILIKE against name, email, and company rather than vector search. Deliberate: when I search for a person I know their name, and exact matching is predictable in a way semantic search is not. Semantic search over a contacts table mostly produces confusing near-misses.

title: Task status model
content: Tasks have three states: pending, in_progress, done. Resisted adding more because every extra state is one I would have to remember to move things through. Priority is high, medium, low, and due_date is optional. The query for what's on my plate pulls pending and in_progress together, which is the only view I use.

title: Portfolio needs the eval work
content: The retrieval evaluation work is more differentiating on a profile than the agent itself. Anyone can wire up an agent framework. Very few can show a labelled set, a baseline number committed to version control, and an honest account of which changes did not help. Worth writing up properly rather than burying in a repo.

title: Repo visibility for judging
content: The submission repo has to be reachable by judges. Public is simplest. If kept private, judge accounts have to be added as collaborators individually, which is fragile and easy to get wrong under time pressure. Decision: make the submission repo public and keep anything sensitive out of it entirely rather than relying on access control.

title: Nothing sensitive in the repo
content: The repo has no credentials, no tokens, and no service account keys. .gitignore covers .env and all JSON except agent.json. Local notes and demo assets are also excluded. This matters more than usual because the repo goes public for hackathon judging, so anything committed is committed permanently and publicly.

title: Postgres and pgvector basics worth remembering
content: The vector extension provides the distance operators: <=> is cosine distance, <-> is L2, <#> is negative inner product. Cosine is the right one for normalised embeddings. A vector column declares its dimension and rejects anything else, which is what caught the 384 versus 768 mistake. Same operators work on AlloyDB.

title: Search returns five results, hard-coded
content: search_notes has LIMIT 5 written into the query. Never thought about that number. If six notes are relevant the sixth is dropped silently, with no signal to me or to the model that it happened. Flagging as something the eval should tell me about rather than something to change on instinct.

title: Citations must name the note, not the chunk
content: If retrieval starts returning chunks instead of whole notes, a chunk id means nothing to me. Every chunk has to resolve to its parent note id and title. If several chunks of the same note come back they should collapse into one citation. And deleting a note must delete its chunks, which is a foreign key with cascade rather than something I remember to do.

title: Hybrid search idea
content: Dense retrieval handles paraphrase well and exact rare terms badly. Searching for a specific error string or a platform name like OneBullex is exactly where embeddings are weakest and plain keyword matching is strongest. Postgres has full text search built in, so combining the two costs no new infrastructure. Candidate for the reranking work rather than a separate project.

title: Weekly review habit
content: Trying a weekly review: what shipped, what is blocked, what deadline moved closer. The value is not the list, it is noticing when something has been blocked for three weeks without me registering it. The pricing of my attention is the scarce thing, not the number of hours.

title: Hack2Skills portal quirks
content: The Hack2Skills portal saves partial submissions but does not warn you if a required field is empty until you hit submit. Also the file upload silently fails on large videos rather than showing an error. Compress the video before uploading and verify the submission actually shows as complete rather than trusting the confirmation screen.

title: Interview question I keep getting
content: Asked repeatedly how I would scale SmartDesk to multiple users. Honest answer is that it is currently single-user and the OAuth token storage is the blocker: tokens are process-wide on the instance, so two users on the same container could see each other's credentials. Saying that plainly has gone better than pretending the design is multi-tenant.

title: Session state is per-session not per-user
content: ADK session state is keyed to a session, not to a user identity. For a single-user project that distinction never surfaces. It becomes a real problem the moment two people use the same deployment, because the auth flags I keep in state are not scoped to a person. Noting it so I do not forget the assumption is baked in.

title: Why generated eval labels need review
content: If I generate evaluation questions with a language model and then use retrieval driven by the same family of model to answer them, I risk measuring how well the model agrees with itself rather than whether retrieval works. Generated labels are candidates. They need reading and correcting before any number derived from them means anything.

title: Small eval sets cannot resolve small effects
content: With thirty questions, one question is worth about three points of recall at one. So a change that moves recall by two points is indistinguishable from noise. Either accept that the eval can only detect large effects, or grow the set. Reporting a two point gain from thirty questions as an improvement would be self-deception.

title: Laptop constraints shape the tooling
content: 16GB, no GPU. That rules out running anything large locally and is why development uses a small CPU embedding model rather than anything heavier. It is also why the cloud database stays off unless actively needed. Constraints are fine as long as the code does not assume otherwise.

title: No LangChain or LlamaIndex
content: Deliberately not using a retrieval framework. The stack is ADK plus plain SQL, and adding a framework on top would hide exactly the mechanics I am trying to understand. BM25 is twenty lines. Reciprocal rank fusion is five. Writing them means I know what they do when a number moves.

title: Three tracks in one project
content: The hackathon awards points across three tracks and SmartDesk hits all three with one project rather than three features bolted together. Track 1 is the ADK agent framework and Cloud Run deployment. Track 2 is MCP for Gmail and Calendar. Track 3 is AlloyDB with vector search. The orchestration is what ties them into one thing.

title: Backup and recovery for accounts
content: Recovery options are set on all four accounts and they do not point at each other in a cycle, which would be useless if I lost access to one. Recovery codes for the important accounts are stored offline. The failure mode I am guarding against is losing the phone, not losing a password.

title: add_note has to keep indexes in sync
content: If retrieval ever uses chunks, then adding a note has to write both the whole-note embedding and the note's chunks in the same operation. Otherwise notes added after the switch are invisible to chunk-based retrieval and I would not notice until a search silently missed something recent. Worst kind of bug: quiet and delayed.

title: Overfitting to your own eval set
content: If I tune chunk size, overlap, and fusion weights by maximising performance on the same thirty questions I evaluate on, I am fitting noise and the number stops meaning anything. Any real tuning needs a held-out set. Until then, better to leave parameters at sensible defaults and say so.

title: Judging criteria weighting
content: Scoring weights innovation, technical implementation, and use of the sponsor stack. Demo quality matters more than it should, in the sense that a working demo of a simpler thing beats a broken demo of a sophisticated one. Which argues for making the demo path bulletproof rather than adding one more feature.

Worth deciding well before month eleven whether it is going ahead, because deciding late means either rushing it or losing the priority date by default.

title: Full architecture and decision log
content: Consolidated record of how SmartDesk ended up as it is. Framing: a single chat interface over email, calendar, and a personal knowledge base, built solo for a hackathon and used by exactly one person, me. Agent layer. A root orchestrator handles authentication and routes to one of three sub-agents using ADK's transfer_to_agent. inbox_agent talks to Gmail, planner_agent to Calendar, data_agent to the knowledge base. This split came after a single-agent version with a dozen tools kept selecting the wrong one; splitting by domain made routing reliable. Each sub-agent formats its own output, so there is no separate response formatting step. Model choice is gemini-2.5-flash throughout, on the grounds that routing and formatting do not need deeper reasoning and Flash keeps the interaction responsive. Integration layer. Gmail and Calendar are reached through self-hosted MCP servers launched as stdio subprocesses. The hosted HTTP MCP endpoints were tried first and abandoned because the authentication path was not available to me. Running the servers locally means I own the OAuth flow and can debug by reading their output. Data layer. AlloyDB in production, Postgres with pgvector in development, same schema. Notes carry a 768 dimension embedding from text-embedding-005, retrieved by cosine distance. Contacts and tasks use ordinary filters, because exact matching is what I actually want when looking up a person or listing what is outstanding. The single portability problem was AlloyDB's in-database embedding function, which stock Postgres lacks; computing embeddings client-side and binding the vector as a parameter solved it for both. Known weaknesses, written down rather than hidden. OAuth tokens are stored in a process-wide file, which is fine for one user and unacceptable for two. Retrieval returns a hard-coded five results and nobody chose that number. Retrieval quality is unmeasured, which means every improvement to it would be a guess. Session state is scoped per session rather than per user. Deployment. Container on Cloud Run in us-central1, matching the Vertex region. Scales to zero, which is what makes running it affordable. The image was reduced from 1.8GB to 340MB after cold starts of 8 to 12 seconds made the first request unusable.

The switching cost between them is the real problem, and it is the honest reason SmartDesk exists at all: it is a tool for the specific mess described in this note.

title: Retrieval improvement plan in full
content: Plan for improving notes retrieval, in the order the work should happen, with the reasoning for the order. The problem. search_notes embeds each note whole with text-embedding-005, stores a 768 dimension vector, retrieves by cosine distance, and returns a hard-coded five results. There is no chunking, no reranking, and no evaluation. Whether this is good is unknown, and therefore whether any change to it is an improvement is also unknown. Stage one, evaluation, before touching anything. A labelled set of questions mapped to the notes that genuinely answer them. Metrics: recall at k, since the agent reads several results and can synthesise across them, and mean reciprocal rank, since a model weights the first thing it reads far more heavily than the fifth. Report at several cutoffs. Commit a baseline number to version control so every later change is measured against something fixed rather than against memory. Nothing in the pipeline changes at this stage, which is precisely the point and also why it is tempting to skip. Stage two, chunking. Token-based with configurable size and overlap, aligned to sentence boundaries so citations read properly, with every chunk linked to its parent note by foreign key so a chunk hit resolves to something I recognise. A separate table, additive, leaving the notes table and its embedding untouched so the existing path keeps working and the migration is safe to apply to a live database. The honest expectation is that this helps on long notes and does nothing on short ones, and my notes are mostly short. If it does not help, that result gets reported rather than buried. Stage three, reranking. Retrieve a wider candidate set, then reorder it and return the top few. Compare something cheap and lexical against something LLM-based, and report accuracy, latency, and cost together, because a reranker that adds two seconds to save one rank position is not obviously worth it. Open questions I have not resolved. Whether questions generated from the notes will be phrased too much like the source text and inflate the scores. Whether recall or MRR should be the headline number. And whether an eval set of thirty questions can resolve the differences I am chasing at all, which I suspect it cannot.

title: Notes on evaluating anything subjective
content: Longer thinking on why measurement keeps being the thing that matters. The pattern I keep hitting is that systems whose quality is subjective and whose changes are frequent will drift without anyone noticing, because there is no number that moves when they get worse. Retrieval is the clearest case. A search that returns confident, plausible, wrong results looks identical to one that works, right up until someone checks. Nobody checks, because checking is boring and the system never complains. What a usable evaluation needs. A labelled set, which is the expensive part and the part that cannot be automated away, because labels generated by a model and then used to evaluate that model measure agreement rather than correctness. A metric that matches how the output is actually consumed: recall if a model reads several results, rank-sensitive metrics if it weights the first heavily, and both if both are true. A committed baseline, so that improvement is a comparison rather than an impression. And some sense of the resolution: with a small labelled set, only large effects are detectable, and reporting small ones as real is self-deception dressed up as rigour. Where this applies beyond retrieval. The natural language query idea, where the correctness of generated SQL is measurable against labelled examples. Agent routing, where the correct sub-agent for a given request is itself a label and mis-routing is currently invisible. Both of those are today evaluated by trying them a few times and forming an impression, which is exactly the failure mode described above. The uncomfortable part. Building the harness produces no visible improvement on its own, which makes it the easiest work to skip and the hardest to justify while it is happening. The payoff only appears later, when a change that felt like an improvement turns out not to be, and knowing that early is worth more than the change would have been.

title: Submission checklist, complete
content: Everything that has to be true before the hackathon submission is done, gathered so nothing is discovered missing at the deadline. Repository. Public, or every judge account added individually, which is fragile enough that public is the right choice. No credentials, tokens, or service account keys anywhere in the history, not just the current tree, since a public repo makes anything ever committed permanently public. README that explains what the project is and how to run it, written for someone who has never seen it. Deployment. Service deployed to Cloud Run and confirmed reachable from a browser that is not signed into my account. Cold start acceptable, or minimum instances raised for the judging window and lowered afterwards so the cost is bounded to a few days. The demo URL in the submission must be the one actually deployed, checked by opening it rather than assumed. OAuth consent screen test users updated, since an unverified app rejects anyone not on the list, and a judge hitting a 403 will not debug it for me. Deck. Exactly the official 11-slide template, in their section order, with their problem statement wording rather than my own framing, because scoring is section by section against the template. Video. Within the length limit, compressed enough to upload without the silent failure the portal does on large files, showing one continuous flow that demonstrates orchestration across all three tracks rather than three disconnected features. Portal. Submitted through Hack2Skills, not email. Every required field filled, verified by the submission showing as complete rather than by trusting the confirmation screen. Uploaded a full day early, treating the stated deadline as two hours earlier than it says. Account correctness, which is the one that has bitten me before. Registration is under the professional account. The GCP project is under the main account. These are different accounts, and the submission must reference the project the judges can actually reach.

title: Things deliberately not built
content: Recording what was consciously left out, so I do not rediscover these as gaps later and assume they were oversights. A frontend. SmartDesk is an ADK service, reachable through adk web or an HTTP request. No custom UI, and none planned. Multi-user support. Single-user by design. The OAuth token scoping and the session state assumptions both bake this in and would need real work to undo. Vector indexing. Sequential scan is exact and fast enough at this corpus size, whereas approximate indexes trade recall for speed I do not need yet. A retrieval framework. No LangChain, no LlamaIndex, because they would hide the mechanics I am trying to learn. Mobile anything. Nobody has asked, including me.

title: What good looks like in three months
content: Hackathon submitted and judged, whatever the outcome. Retrieval measured, with a number I trust and an honest account of which changes helped and which did not. Patent decision made deliberately rather than by running out of clock. Job search either converted or wound down rather than left drifting. And the four-inbox situation either genuinely under control or consciously accepted, rather than being a low-grade tax I keep paying without deciding to.

title: Withdrawal address whitelisting
content: Enabled address whitelisting on the exchange accounts so withdrawals can only go to addresses I have pre-approved, with a time delay before a new address becomes usable. This is the control that actually limits damage if credentials leak, more than 2FA does, because it caps where funds can go rather than just who can log in.

title: Dockerfile slimming details
content: The image went from 1.8GB to 340MB by switching from the full Python image to the slim variant and not installing build tooling in the final layer. The dependencies that pulled the most weight were the Google client libraries. Nothing was removed functionally, it was all base image and build cruft.

title: Region choice for Cloud Run
content: Deployed to us-central1 rather than an Asia region despite being closer to Asia, because that is where the Vertex model endpoints I use are available and cross-region calls to Vertex would add more latency than the user-to-service hop saves. If model availability changes this is worth revisiting.

title: Service account roles needed
content: The Cloud Run service account needs Vertex AI User to call Gemini and the embedding model, and AlloyDB Client to reach the database. Started with an over-broad role and narrowed it once things worked. Narrowing after the fact is easier than debugging permission errors during initial setup.

title: adk web for local development
content: Local development uses adk web, which serves a dev UI on localhost and hot-reloads the agent. This is the fastest loop for testing prompt and routing changes. It is a development tool, not the product, and is not what gets deployed.

title: Prompt changes need re-testing routing
content: Every time I edit the root agent's instruction, routing behaviour can change in ways that are not obvious. Adding a clarifying sentence about calendar once caused notes queries to start routing to the planner agent. There is no test for this, which is a gap. Routing correctness is itself a labelling problem.

title: Suppressing noisy SDK warnings
content: The Google SDKs emit warnings about non-text parts in responses and about experimental features on almost every call, which buries real errors. Filtering them at import time in both agent.py and tools.py. Slightly risky in that it could hide something real, so the filters are narrow rather than blanket.

title: Video length limit is strict
content: The demo video has a hard length limit and going over means rejection rather than a deduction. My first cut ran long because I explained the architecture verbally. Cut the explanation and let the demo show it, which was better anyway. Architecture belongs in the deck, not the video.

title: What judges actually see first
content: Realistically judges open the demo URL and the video before reading anything. If the URL is slow or broken, nothing else recovers it. That argues for spending the last day on verifying the deployed demo works from a clean browser rather than on polishing the deck.

title: Second hackathon on DoraHacks
content: Separate hackathon tracked on DoraHacks under the technical account. Different submission model: a BUIDL page rather than a form, so the write-up lives on their platform and has to be maintained there rather than in the repo. Deadlines are independent of the Google Cloud one, which is the actual risk since I keep conflating them.

title: Do not conflate the two hackathon deadlines
content: Two hackathons in flight on two platforms under two accounts with two different deadlines. Wrote them both down explicitly after nearly working toward the wrong one. Hack2Skills for the Google Cloud one on the professional account, DoraHacks on the technical account.

title: Tracking which resume version went where
content: Each application records role, company, date sent, and resume version. Without the version field I could not answer what a specific employer had actually seen, which came up in an interview and was embarrassing. The tracking lives with the application notes, not in a separate spreadsheet.

title: Talking about failures in interviews
content: The strongest interview material has been the bugs, not the features. The duplicate response bug required understanding why ADK's loop does not terminate on a null response. The token scoping issue required noticing a security problem in my own design. Both are more convincing than a feature list.

title: Profiles that need updating
content: LinkedIn on the professional account, plus profiles on the job platforms tied to the applications account. They have drifted apart, which looks careless if anyone checks both. Consolidating the wording so the same three things lead everywhere: multi-agent orchestration, MCP integration, and measured retrieval quality.

title: GenAI Academy pacing
content: The Academy content is self-paced, which means it competes with the hackathon deadline rather than supporting it. The codelabs that directly feed the build are worth doing now. The rest is worth deferring until after submission rather than doing everything in order.

title: MCP is simpler than it looks
content: MCP is a protocol for exposing tools to a model over a transport. The stdio transport is just a subprocess reading and writing JSON on stdin and stdout. Once that clicked, writing the Gmail and Calendar servers was straightforward. The complexity in the docs is mostly about the hosted and HTTP cases.

title: Cosine distance versus similarity
content: pgvector's <=> returns cosine distance, where smaller is closer. Similarity is 1 minus that. Ordering by distance ascending and reporting 1 minus distance as a similarity score is the usual pattern, and mixing the two up produces a ranking that is exactly backwards, which is an easy mistake to make and an obvious one once seen.

title: Why overlap matters in chunking
content: Without overlap, a fact that straddles a chunk boundary appears in neither chunk intact, so no single embedding represents it. Overlap repeats the tail of one chunk at the head of the next so boundary-straddling content survives somewhere. The cost is storage and some duplicate results, which is why chunks have to collapse to parent notes.

title: Session hygiene in Claude Code web
content: The container is discarded when the session ends, so uncommitted work is lost. Rule: commit and push before stopping, even mid-task, even if the commit message is rough. A rough commit that exists beats a clean one that does not.

title: Deadline reminders need lead time not accuracy
content: A reminder on the deadline itself is useless. The useful reminder is at whatever lead time the work actually takes, which for the patent non-provisional is months and for a hackathon upload is a day. Setting reminders by work required rather than by date is the change that made this stop failing.

title: Cost discipline on a personal project
content: The rules that keep this affordable: cloud database off unless actively testing, Cloud Run scales to zero, no minimum instances except during judging, and development against local Postgres with a local embedding model. Everything expensive is opt-in rather than always-on.

title: Platform UI can disagree with the chain
content: Learned to verify transactions on Etherscan rather than trusting a platform's own display, after a balance showed as updated on one platform before the transaction had actually confirmed. The chain is the source of truth and the platform UI is a cache that can be stale or wrong.

title: Keep exchange accounts off the main inbox
content: Exchange accounts are on the technical account rather than the main one specifically so that a compromise of my everyday inbox does not immediately reach the accounts with money in them. The Etherscan placement on the professional account breaks this pattern, though it is read-only so the exposure is low.

title: What the provisional actually protects
content: A provisional does not itself grant anything. It establishes a priority date and lets me use patent pending language. The protection only materialises if a non-provisional follows within twelve months. Treating the provisional as if it were protection is the mistake to avoid.

title: SMT and the patent overlap
content: The SMT work and the provisional filing are related, which is why both correspondence streams land on the technical account. Keeping them on one account is deliberate rather than accidental, unlike the Etherscan placement.

title: What search_notes returns to the model
content: Each result is id, title, content, and a similarity score. The model weaves these into prose and cites the title. If retrieval moves to chunks, the shape has to stay compatible or the agent's formatting breaks, which means chunk results must still carry the parent note's id and title in the same fields.

title: Error handling in tools
content: Database errors are caught and returned as a dict with an error key rather than raised, so the agent can tell the user something went wrong instead of the whole turn failing. Internal callers like the eval harness need the opposite: errors should be loud, because a silently empty result set corrupts a measurement.

title: Tasks query pulls two statuses
content: The what's on my plate view needs both pending and in_progress, since something started but unfinished is still on my plate. Ordering is by priority then due date. This is the only tasks view I use, so it is the one worth getting right.

title: Demo flow must show orchestration
content: A demo showing three features one after another looks like three scripts. The version that lands shows a single request that requires the orchestrator to route across domains, so the multi-agent structure is visible rather than asserted. That is the whole premise of the track.

title: The actual problem SmartDesk solves
content: Four inboxes, two hackathon platforms, three trading platforms, a patent clock, and a job search, none of which talk to each other. The cost is not any single task, it is that nothing can answer what is closest to a deadline across all of them. That is the specific problem, and it is mine rather than hypothetical.

title: Null results are worth reporting
content: A change that does not help is information, provided it was measured. Reporting it preserves trust in the numbers that did move, and prevents someone later re-trying the same thing. Quietly keeping a change that did not help is how a system accumulates complexity with no corresponding benefit.

title: Where the eval harness lives
content: The harness, the labelled question set, the corpus, and the committed results all live under evals/ in the repo rather than in a notebook or a scratch directory. Reason: a number that is not in version control cannot be compared against later, and a harness someone else cannot run is not reproducible.
